_doc: T-3645: every "why" a building's floating card folds behind its button (tools/reading_why.mjs), retold for younger readers. Keyed by the note's own words; a note the Details tab shows too is told in the notes file. Only the younger ages are written; no fact enters that the note does not hold, and the build's own talk (record ids, kit names, pixel and camera readings) is left out, so a young reader gets what was read and from where, and what is a guess.

8-10: An old map calls this the soldiers' garden and the town's corn field. A book by Quaife says the land was dug up to grow the garden and the corn. The map says it was corn. That the corn stood tall in August is our guess: corn put in by May is tall by then. The fence is part of this place. The corn and the garden rows are drawn by our garden maker. The corn grows in small hills, four plants each. The soldiers' rows are in the north-east corner. Before that, the ground inside was bare.

It is 17 by 12 feet. We read that off the old map, the same way we read every building outside the fort. It may be smaller, since the map draws the roof and the front as one. In 1800 Du Sable sold his farm to Jean La Lime. Someone told us the paper of that sale lists the house, two barns, a horse mill, a bake house, a hen house, a milk house and a smoke house. We could not get that paper, so we did not use it. No size here comes from it. We did not build the horse and the pole it pulls. No paper says if the horse walked inside or outside.

It is 23 by 16 feet. We read that off the old map, the same way we read every building outside the fort. The map draws a small picture of the roof and front as one, so it may be less deep. Its long side runs along the river bank. Which house was La Lime's and which was Le Mai's, how big they were, and when they closed, are all still our guesses.

It is 24 by 13 feet. We read that off the old map, the same way we read every building outside the fort. The map draws a small picture of the roof and front as one, so it may be less deep. Its long side runs along the river bank. Which house was La Lime's and which was Le Mai's, how big they were, and when they closed, are all still our guesses.

It is 3 meters wide. That is the least we can build, with a gate at each end. No paper gives the width. This part is about 19 meters long. It is one of four parts. The ground slopes down to the river, so the walk is cut in steps. Under this part the ground drops a little. The fort's dock and the covered walk to the river stand where one old map and one line in a book put them.

No size here comes from it. The size is our own guess for a small log milk house.

It is 5.5 by 3.8 meters, or 18 by 12 feet. In 1800 Du Sable sold his farm to Jean La Lime. Someone told us the paper of that sale lists the house, two barns, a horse mill, a bake house, a hen house, a milk house and a smoke house. We could not get that paper, so we did not use it. No size here comes from it. The size is our own guess. It leaves room for an oven and a work floor. It is low enough to sit by the west end of the house, as the old pictures show.

It is 6.6 by 6.2 meters, or 22 by 20 feet. No paper gives its size. In a picture by Eastman its end is about as wide as the east end of the house. Its long side holds a row of stalls. In 1800 Du Sable sold his farm to Jean La Lime. Someone told us the paper of that sale lists the house, two barns, a horse mill, a bake house, a hen house, a milk house and a smoke house. We could not get that paper, so we did not use it. Our size for the barn does not come from it.

The walk is open at both ends. Each end is a gate between short bits of fence. The old map does not draw the covered walk, and shows no way into it from the fort. We added a small back gate through both rows of the fort's fence. It leads into the walk. That gate is our guess.

We took this roof from a picture by Currey. The owner of this project chose it. The picture, from 1912, shows a small building in the fort's north-east corner. Its roof comes to a point, with four sides. Only the roof shows over the fence in that picture, so the roof is all it tells us. The owner looked at the picture and an old map from 1808, building by building. The owner took the pointed roof from the picture and kept the map for all the rest. The picture was made long after the fort was gone, from an old model. It is not drawn to size. So the slope of the roof, the size of the building and the height of the walls are our guesses. None of them is read off the picture. The 1808 map shows the building and where it stood, but not its roof. Before the owner chose, the roof was a plain two-sided one, and that was a guess too.

This says where the chimneys sit along the top of the roof. A picture from 1857 puts one chimney near the middle and one near the east end. A drawing by Lossing has the middle one too, but puts his second one near the west end. Three of the four old pictures put the second chimney toward the east. So we built the chimneys where the 1857 picture puts them. We wrote down that Lossing's picture does not agree.

We read this from words, not a drawing. The old map's list names a covered way to get water, but says it was left off the map. A book by Quaife says a covered way ran from the fort's north-east corner to the river. So our walk starts at that corner of the outer fence. It runs north to the river, about 26 meters away. A check makes sure each part steps down only a little and that the last part reaches the water. Where it runs and how its parts fit are our guesses.

The old map calls this the Interpreter's House. It was the home of the man who spoke for the fort with the Native people. It stood west of the fort. We do not know who lived in it in 1812. A doctor at the fort put La Lime, the interpreter, in a house north of the river in 1808. La Lime was killed in the spring of 1812. We put no one in it.

The old map calls this the armorer's shop. The armorer fixed the soldiers' guns. We read its number, 20, beside it on the map. We call it a work shop, not a store. It was the army's, not a business, so it has no sign.

The old map calls this a house of the trading post. We read its number, 23, beside it. The buildings north and south of it are 24, the stables. It belonged to the government's trading house. We do not know what it was used for, so we call it a shed. We first built it as a stable. Now it has a new name, but it has not moved.

This ground was part of Kinzie's Addition, the land north of the river. The state's old book of land sales lists it. It is about 102 acres, not the usual 160, since the river cuts it. We drew its edges from the survey lines and the river bank, not by hand. The book lists the land twice, the same sale both times. It spells the buyer two ways: Robert A Kenzie and Robert A Kinzie. We keep both, since two spellings may or may not be one man. This building stands 42 meters inside the edge of the land. Our lines could be off by about 20 meters, so it is safe inside. The book says this man bought the land. It does not say he still owned it in 1835, that he lived here, or that he ever stood on it. The survey lines are our own. We drew them from one old corner at State and Madison, in squares a mile wide.

We measured this garden with the old map's own scale, 50 feet to an inch. That reading of the scale is our guess. Its four sides make a box 229 by 115 feet. The map's lines were drawn by hand, so the box is our guess too.

A book by Moses and Kirkland says: 'The house was of squared logs, after the fashion of the very best of the frontier mansions of that day.' That tells us the logs. It does not say they were left dark. We kept the squared logs. Painting them white is our own choice. We did not add boards on the outside, and we did not make up a date for any.

No paper says where the Miami men camped. We chose this ground. Old accounts say only that Wells came from Fort Wayne with about thirty Miami men on ponies. On the 15th they marched out, some in front of the soldiers and some behind. Men on horses, come to lead the soldiers out, would camp near the fort. They would be near its stables and the road south. They would be apart from the Potawatomi camp by the creek. So we put the camp on flat prairie, about 40 meters south of the fort's stables. The owner of this project asked for the camps to go where they most likely were. The ground here is flat. The camp keeps clear of every building, path and road.

No old picture shows people living up under the roof, or a window on the roof. One picture by Sarony shows a small window at the end of the roof, and we built it. It does not mean anyone lived up there. An old note said no picture showed such a window. That note was wrong, and we fixed it.

No paper says what this house was built of. We say logs. Every house at the fort before 1812 that the old books describe was made of logs. That includes the Kinzie house, the agent's house, the trading house, Lee's Place and the cabin Hurlbut thought was this one. So we built it of logs. That is our guess, and we wrote it down.

No paper says what it was made of. We built it of wood like the rest of the fort. We used boards, not logs. It is so small that log corners would almost meet in the middle of the walls. A book by Quaife says only that it was wood.

It first shows on 25 January 1808, the date on an old map of the fort by Whistler. That is the first time anyone draws this house. It may be older. One account says Ouilmette lived at Chicago from 1790. Mrs. Whistler counted his house as one of four huts in 1803. Old books say it still stood in August 1812. The book Wau-Bun says Mrs. Helm hid in it on the 16th. The next day a soldier climbed in at its back window. Currey says this family was the only one in the village that did not leave home. Hubbard came in 1818. He listed every building in the area, and he still lists Ouilmette's cabin north of the river. We end the cabin on 31 December 1829. Ouilmette moved away to Gross Pointe in the late 1820s. No paper shows the cabin after that. So it is not in the 1835 town.
One chimney. A picture from 1912 draws it outside one end of the house. It is the left end, seen from the river, at the front corner.

A picture from 1893 by Kurz and Allison draws each of the fort's two towers with a small lookout on the roof and no chimney. We had built one chimney, but that was only our guess. We took it away to match the picture. The picture was made long after, so it does not prove there was no chimney. The lookout, and where the picture puts the towers, are still not sure. We did not move anything else. The full count of chimneys in 1812 is still our guess.

An old map from 1808 says the soldiers' houses were two floors high, with porches facing the yard. It does not say how many porch floors there were. A picture by Currey from 1912 shows a covered walk up top, with a rail, over an open porch below. So we built two porch floors here too. That is our guess for this building. How deep the porch is, its posts, floors, rail and roof are our guesses too. Where a post would hit a window, we moved it to the nearest solid wall. Nothing else moved. We do not say there was a door to the top porch.

An old picture by Sarony shows the front fence and the window at the end of the roof in light colors. Currey says his picture covers 1804 to 1813 and 1816 to 1828. A picture by Eastman from 1820 also shows that end window. None of these says the house was painted white in August 1812. We painted the logs white, but that is our guess. We do not say it had boards on the outside. We used to think every light picture meant boards were added later. That was only a guess, and we took it out. The cut logs still show.

In Sarony's picture, the door at the west end is taller than our first door. Its top was about level with the window next to it. So we made the door 2.5 meters tall, with a low step. That matches the picture better. The wall is 3 meters tall, so the door cannot be taller than that. Its height is our guess, not a measure. The door's width and place, the front door and the other windows did not change.

The owner of this project looked at a picture by Currey. Each side of the tower's little roof has a small dark hole, to look out far. The picture shows two sides of each roof with one hole each. We gave the other two sides one each too. The picture is too small to show their shape or size. So we built each as a small framed hole under a little roof. Their size and place are our guesses.

The owner of this project looked at the pictures. The lookout on top of the tower is made of logs, like the rest of the tower, not boards. Currey's picture draws it with the same rows as the walls below. Men building the towers of logs would build the lookout the same way. How thick the logs are and how they meet are our own, like the rest of the tower. The pictures do not measure them.

The owner of this project chose this roof. A picture by Currey from 1912 shows the gunpowder hut with a round roof. That fits an old map from 1808, which draws an arched front. We use that roof shape for the first fort in 1812 only. The pictures do not say how big the curve is, how thick, what color, or when it was built. Where the hut stands, which way it faces and how wide it is did not change. The pictures do not measure it.

We placed this behind the west end of the house, the way three pictures draw it. We did not measure it. Three pictures, all made from across the river, show a low building with a chimney just behind the west end. Its far end sticks out a little past the house. Working from the pictures, its corner falls 0 to 3 meters west of the house. We set it in the middle, about 1.3 meters. The pictures cannot show how far back it is. So we set it just clear of the back of the house. We moved a tree 3.5 meters north to make room. Which building is which in the pictures, and where the rest stand, are our guesses.

We placed this ourselves, in the shade behind the house. Wau-Bun says only that the buildings stood around the house. No picture shows a milk house. From across the river, the house and its trees hide this spot. A milk house needs shade and should be near the kitchen door. So we put it between the two big trees, just behind the house. That is our guess.

We placed this from two old accounts and the shape of the ground. We did not measure it. Wau-Bun says the house was on the north bank of the river, right across from the fort. Currey says it was near where Pine Street ends, facing south with the river in front. So the house lines up with the fort's flag pole. It is set back from the river bank. The same book tells of a big green yard between the house and the river. We left 18 meters of green between the porch and the top of the bank. How far back the house sits is our guess.

We placed this field by a rule, not a measure. The old map does not draw things outside the fort to size. So we take where the map puts the field, next to the Kinzie house, and spread it out. We spread it about two and a half times. That comes from a fence the man says was 52 yards long, set against how long he drew it. The other houses on that bank stand by the same rule, so the field stays in its place by them. On the map the field is drawn at a slant, and we kept the slant. A check makes sure the field is where the rule puts it, not in the river and not on a house. Which way is east on the map is our guess too.

We did not measure where this stands. The old map draws the fort to size, but says the buildings outside it are not drawn to size. So we take where the map puts it, and spread that out from the fort's main gate. We spread it two and a half times. That comes from the scale written on the garden, 50 feet to an inch, against the fort's 20. A check makes sure the place is what this rule gives. The rule is our guess. The man who drew the map gives two distances that do not agree with each other: one spreads the map out about three times, the other about seven.

We placed this on a line from Eastman's picture. We did not measure it. Eastman's picture from 1820 shows a low white house with a door and a window. It is just right of the stable and behind it. Its far end shows, and its near end is hidden by the stable roof. So it stands a little north of the stable and farther off. No other picture shows it. From across the river the house and a big tree hide it. How far along that line it stands is our guess.

We placed this where lines from two pictures cross. We did not measure it. Eastman drew a picture in 1820 from up the bank to the east. It shows a low log building in front of the east end of the Kinzie house, with horses by it. Sarony made a picture from Juliette Kinzie's sketch, from across the river. It shows a small building east of the house, behind a row of trees. Two later pictures put it in the same place. The lines from the two pictures cross about 21 meters east and 14 meters north of the house's corner. So the building stands there. The later pictures show a white building with a window in its end. That does not fit Eastman's log stable. So it may have been changed by about 1831, or a new one built there. Eastman drew his picture on the spot in 1820, so we built the stable as he drew it. Its place is our guess.

The plan from 1808 shows a small lookout on top of both towers. But its notes say they were not built yet. A picture from 1893 shows a small lookout on each tower and no chimney. A picture by Currey from 1912 shows a small square lookout with a pointed roof on both towers. The plan, and the two later pictures, are why we think they were done before the fort burned in August 1812. No paper says when they were finished. Both pictures were made long after. The note from 1808 shows they were not there in the years before. Every size is our guess. We used the lookout from the second fort, the size the pictures show. We did not build slats, glass or a top knob.

A book by Quaife says the trade agent and the Native agent each had a log house. The Chicago Magazine of March 1857 also says the trading house was two floors of logs. A web page quotes it. We can name that page, but we do not know if we may use it, so we did not build from it.

We read this from Sarony's picture. The porch posts are about 3 meters tall, and so is the edge of the porch roof. Another old picture shows the same. Every post is much taller than the 2 meter posts we first built. So the posts are nearly as tall as the 3 meter wall, as the old prints show. The top beam is just under 3 meters.

We placed these hay stacks across the river from the cabin. We did not measure them. Wau-Bun says only that the stacks were on the far bank from the cabin. A soldier walked down to the canoes, pointed to them over the water, and soon got to them. The river there was narrow, with woods close behind. We put the cabin on the north-west bank, so the stacks are on the south-east bank. There are four stacks in a loose group, 42 to 62 meters from the river. There are 8 to 12 meters of grass between them. That leaves room for cows to stand among them, and for two men to walk round them out of sight. Every distance is our guess. If the river moves, the stacks move with it.

We placed this by a rule, not a measure. Whistler's map draws three houses west of Kinzie's, each marked 31, as other houses across the river. He says the places outside the fort are not drawn to size. Our rule spreads the map out from the main gate. Here we spread it out from the Kinzie house instead. From the gate, these houses would land east of the Kinzie house, but the map draws them west of it. We spread it two and a half times. That comes from a fence the man says was 52 yards long, drawn on this bank between two of the houses. The other number would set the houses too far apart for that fence. The house faces south to the river, as the map draws its front. A check makes sure it is not in the water or on another house. Which house was La Lime's and which Le Mai's, their size and when they closed, are our guesses.

We placed this by a rule, not a measure. Whistler's map draws three houses west of Kinzie's, each marked 31, as other houses across the river. He says the places outside the fort are not drawn to size. We spread the north bank out from the Kinzie house, two and a half times, using a fence the man says was 52 yards long. This is the smallest of the three houses and the nearest to Kinzie's. That is why we say it was Ouilmette's. Currey says his cabin was close behind the Kinzie house. Wau-Bun says it was close at hand. Our rule puts it a little behind the Kinzie house and 30 meters west. That fits, so we did not move it. A check makes sure it is not in the water or on another house.

We placed this by a rule, not a measure. Whistler's map names number 32 as an old mill for grain, worked by horses. Someone found it on the map, between the eastern house marked 31 and Kinzie's garden. We could not get the map this time to read it again, so we used that reading. We spread it out from the Kinzie house, the same way as the houses marked 31. It faces the river, like the other houses on that bank. A check makes sure it is not in the water or on another house. Which building is which, and where the rest stand, are our guesses.

We placed this dock on our river, not where the old map draws it. The map draws it as a small dotted shape west of the fort, by the words '122 feet to River'. But the map also says the river was not measured with care. So we kept only his distance and his side. We went 122 feet out from the fort's north-west corner and found where that meets the river. The dock sits there, along the bank. A check makes sure it has not moved. Where it stands is our guess. It lies across where Kinzie Street would be one day. But no town plan was made until 1830, and the dock is gone after 1812. A street from the future is no reason to move the dock away from its river.

We placed this by an earlier choice, not a measure. We put the farm on the north-west bank of the river, a little below Bridgeport. Hubbard says it was about half a mile below Bridgeport, on the north side of the South Branch. The cabin stands 30 meters back from the river, its long front facing the water. Why near the river? Every account puts the cabin by the water. Wau-Bun says the men's canoes were tied near the bank, in sight of the cabin door. Currey says the farm and the fort talked by canoe. A picture from 1912 draws the house a little back from the bank, inside the fence, with a canoe below. The 30 meters is our guess. The picture gives no distance. The cabin is about 3 miles from the fort, and Heald said about three miles. If the river moves, the cabin moves with it.

All fourteen fort buildings are placed from one point and one direction, so none moves against another. Their sizes come from the fort's own careful plan of 1808, read off it to about a foot. The point is the foot of the flag pole, in the middle of the yard. We set it on the fort's site, read from an old map of 1834. We checked that place against today's landmark, to within 35 meters. That is the site, not the second fort's plan. John H. Kinzie says the first fort stood on the same ground as the last one but was built another way. So we kept the place and nothing of the 1816 fort. The plan has no north arrow. We say its right side is east, since the lake is drawn down that side. That is our guess. The second fort's slant is its own, and we did not borrow it. As a check: our river is about 124 feet from the west side, and the plan says 122 feet. Wilson says 80 feet from the north-west corner, and we have about 65. The whole fort could be off by about 20 meters.

We placed the field with the cabin, by the same choice. Its river side runs 10 meters back from the bank. The cabin stands inside it, 17 meters behind that side. The field runs 30 meters down the river and 120 meters up it, and 90 meters back from the river. Only that there was a field comes from an old paper. Heald says the farm was in a field. Where its edges ran is our guess. A picture from 1912 draws the fence along the bank in front of the house, turning back round a field behind it. We built it that way. The picture gives no sizes.

This is the camp of the gathering in August 1812. Two events date it, not the day it was set up. It starts on 12 August 1812. Wau-Bun says the Native people came from nearby villages, and a meeting was held with them that afternoon. So they were camped by then. Heald's letter says they came from all sides for the trading house's goods. No paper dates the first lodge, so the camp may be older. It stood on the 14th. Currey describes the view from the fort's walls that evening: the Agent's house by the river, and beyond it groups of Native lodges along the creek where State Street is now. It stood on the 15th too. Wau-Bun says Mrs. Helm was led back toward the river, to the camp on its south bank, and into one of the lodges by a stream. It ends on 16 August, the morning the fort was burned. No paper says when the people left after that. The 16th is our choice. It is not in the 1835 town.

Old books say where the camp was. This exact ground is our choice. Currey says the lodges stood in groups along the creek, where State Street is now, on 14 August. Wau-Bun puts the camp on the south bank of the river, with a stream next to it. We had six camp grounds there. Mrs. Helm counted 679 people, and they need more lodges than six grounds can hold. So we added this ground to the group. It is on the flat ground between the group by the river mouth and the horse ground. We picked flat, dry ground. It keeps clear of the creek, the other camps, every building, every path and the 1835 houses. It lies across where Dearborn Street would later be. The town plan came in 1830, eighteen years later. The camp and the street are never in the same year, so we left the camp where it is.

The old map says one window and a door, and we put them in its order. Someone read it closely on the map. From the river, the door is left of the middle, and the window is right of it. So the window is about 2 meters from the east end, and the door about 4 meters. Their sizes are our usual ones.

We read this off the map at its own scale for the Native office's houses, 40 feet to an inch. We read every building outside the fort that way. It comes to about 17 by 19 feet. The map draws a small picture of the roof and front as one, so it may be smaller. The two houses at the fork of the river, and the soldiers' corn field, are our guesses.

We read this off the map at its own scale for the Native office's houses, 40 feet to an inch. We read every building outside the fort that way. It comes to about 15 by 16 feet. The map draws a small picture of the roof and front as one, so it may be smaller. The two houses at the fork of the river, and the soldiers' corn field, are our guesses.

The dock is tied into the bank. Along the bank it is 10 meters, the shortest we can build. The map's mark is about 10 feet long, so our dock is longer than the drawing. That is our guess. Out from the bank, it goes as far as the map's mark shows. It also goes back into the bank, so the deck meets the ground, like the 1835 docks.

There are windows and doors in both ends of the house. On the west end, Sarony draws a small window high under the roof, a window near the back of the wall, and a door near the front with a step. We read their places from his picture. Two other pictures draw the same small window high up. Two more draw something dark high up and a pale mark low on the wall, where Sarony puts his window and door. On the east end, Eastman, in the oldest picture from 1820, draws two small windows side by side, high on the wall. We put them in the log wall, just under the roof. Window and door widths are like the ones on the front. The west door is 2.5 meters tall. None of these sizes was measured long ago.

The far end of this roof slopes down on that side too, as Eastman draws it. The owner of this project chose this. The picture stops the top of the roof over the front right corner. From there the roof falls to the back corner. How far in that slope starts is fitted to the picture. The near end is hidden by the stable's roof, so it keeps a plain end. One small figure in one picture is all we have.

No paper dates this building. In 1831 Juliette Kinzie found these buildings by the house: a milk house, a bake house, a house where the French workers slept, and stables. Eastman's picture from 1820 and three pictures from about 1831 to 1833 show this one. That does not show it in 1812. We say it stood from the fall of 1804, when the Kinzies bought the house, through August 1812, to the end of 1833, with the house it served. Currey says the house was not burned in 1812, and nothing says the yard behind it burned. The family was away from 1812 to 1816. So the later pictures show buildings that stood in 1812, or were built again on the same spot. We chose the first. It goes when the house goes. The house was falling down from 1832 and gone by 1835, so this is not in the 1835 town.

It starts in the fall of 1804. Currey says John Kinzie bought the house from Le Mai that year and came that fall. Other books give other years, so we chose the later one. The house is older than that. Du Sable and Le Mai lived in it before, in a shape no picture shows. It stood in August 1812. Currey says the house was not burned when the others were. It ends at the end of 1833. Currey says it was torn down in the early 1830s. A picture from 1857 shows it about 1833. It was empty and falling down from 1832 and gone by 1835. So it is not in the 1835 town.

The main roof comes down over the porch, with a bend. Some pictures draw one straight roof from the top down to the porch. A picture from 1857 draws a flatter roof under the main one. Sarony's picture, from Juliette Kinzie's own sketch, and Eastman's picture from 1820, the oldest one, both show a bend. The roof gets flatter over the porch. From far off it looks like one roof down to the posts. Up close you see the bend. We built it that way. Before, we had built the 1857 picture's roof.

It starts on 6 April 1812. That evening, a letter by Captain Heald says some men were at Russell and Lee's cabin, in a field by the river. That is the first dated day the cabin is on the ground. It is older, but no paper says by how much. Currey says it was built some time after the fort, so after 1803. It ends at the end of 1822. That is the last year a house stands on the same farm in the old papers. Hubbard says John Crafts had a trading house there, half a mile below Bridgeport, at Hardscrabble. In 1822 Crafts went to work for the fur company. We do not know if Crafts used Lee's cabin or built his own. So the end date is our choice. It is not in the 1835 town either way.

It starts on 7 April 1812. That day Lee's son ran from the farm to warn the fort. Wau-Bun says the family lived in a house on the lake shore, not far from the fort. That is the first dated day for the family, and the house may be older. It was standing on 18 August 1812. Currey lists Charles Lee's house near the mouth of the river as one of four houses left after the fire. Moses and Kirkland say Lee's house south of the fort was sold in 1812 to Jean Baptiste Beaubien. They say nothing of it after that. No paper says when it came down. We end it at the end of 1817, when that old account ends. It is not in the 1835 town. The end date is our guess.

Currey gives the place. This exact ground is our choice. Currey says the Potawatomi liked to camp on the south bank near where the State Street bridge is now, where a creek ran into the river. The mouth of the creek is where the August camp's landing group is. So this ground is on the same bank, a little west of it, by the river. We picked flat, dry ground. It keeps clear of the river, the creek, the camps, every building, every path and the 1835 houses. It lies across where Dearborn Street would later be. The town plan came in 1830, eighteen years later. The camp and the street are never in the same year, so we left the camp where it is.

The place comes from Quaife's words and the old map. Its shape is our choice. Quaife says that near the fork of the river, on the south side, a small field of eight or nine acres was dug up for the soldiers' garden and the town's corn. The map draws it the same way, marked eight acres, on the fort's side of the river where the branch comes in. There is grass land and woods south of it. We laid the field out square, back from both rivers, so no fence can end up in the water. Its edges are not from any old paper. The map's line is drawn freely, not to size. So we set the edges to keep clear of the 1835 buildings that stand here twenty-three years later. It lies across streets of the 1830 town plan. The field was gone after the fort fell in 1812, eighteen years before those streets. Moving it off them would move it away from the fork where Quaife puts it.

Old books say where the camp was. This exact spot is our choice. Currey says the Potawatomi liked to camp on the south bank near where the State Street bridge is now. A small creek opened into the river there and ran back as far as Randolph Street. He says their lodges stood along the creek on the day of our scene. Wau-Bun puts the camp on the south bank of the river with a stream beside it. So the camp is on the creek's banks, never in its bed, in six grounds along it. This one is near the head of the creek, toward Randolph Street. It is the smallest group, the farthest from the fort. Which bank, how far apart, and where each ground sits are our choices. We picked flat ground. Nothing else from 1812 stands on it. Some 1835 houses later stand on parts of it, but never in the same year.

No paper dates this house. It starts on 25 January 1808, the date on Whistler's map, the first time anyone draws it. It may be older. Quaife says there were four houses on the north side from 1803. We say it stood in August 1812, since nothing says it was torn down, burned or left before the soldiers went. It ends on 30 June 1816, the day before the second fort begins. After the war no paper names this house again. Mrs. Callis's list of 1816 names a Mr. Bridges' house that may be one of these, but it is not dated before 1816. It is not in the 1835 town. Which house was La Lime's and which Le Mai's, their size and when they closed, are our guesses.

No paper dates this mill. It starts on 25 January 1808, the date on Whistler's map, whose list already calls it old. It is older than that. The paper of the 1800 sale is said to list a horse mill, but we did not read it. We say it stood in August 1812, since nothing says it was torn down or burned. It ends on 30 June 1816, with the houses beside it. No paper names it after the war. Wau-Bun's list of the Kinzie buildings in 1831 has no mill. Sarony's picture of about 1831 shows only trees and the road where it stood. It is not in the 1835 town.

Two dated stories and a later building give its dates, not a date for this house. It starts on 7 April 1812. That afternoon the warning from Lee's farm was shouted across the river to Burns's house. Soldiers took the mother and her baby, one day old, down to the fort by boat. That is the first day an old book puts the house on the bank. It may be older. It still stood on 18 August 1812. Currey lists it as one of four houses left after the fort and the agent's house burned. Moses and Kirkland say Charles Jouett, the first Native agent, lived in it in 1817. The agent's new house, later called Cobweb Castle, was built near the spot and finished about 1820. So this house ends at the end of 1819. No paper says if the new house was built beside it, on it, or out of it. Ending it then keeps the two from standing at the same time, and keeps it out of the 1835 town.

Two people from 1808 saw it, and we chose when it ends. It starts on 25 January 1808, the date on Whistler's map, the one day an old paper shows it standing. Surgeon Cooper, at the fort from 1808, counts a house near the fork of the river, lived in by a man named Clark who sold cattle. It may be older. No paper we read names it after Cooper's years. So we say it still stood in August 1812, like the La Lime house. It ends on 3 July 1816, the day before the soldiers came back to build the fort again. No account of the new fort names a house at the fork. Its end date is our guess.

No paper dates this work. It starts on 25 January 1808, the date on Whistler's map, whose list names it. It may well be older. These are the first fort's dates, not this part's. It starts on 17 August 1803, the day Swearingen's soldiers reached the bend of the river where the fort would be built. His journal tells of it. It ends on 16 August 1812, the day after the soldiers left, when the fort was burned. No paper dates any one building inside it. The fort was built over the months after they came. Whistler's map of 25 January 1808 is the one day every part here is shown standing. It ends before the second fort of 1816 begins, so the two forts never stand at the same time.

These are the soldiers' dates. It starts on 25 January 1808. That is the date on Whistler's map, the one day an old paper shows the field. It may be older. Soldiers had been at the fort since 1803. It ends on 16 August 1812 with the first fort, the day after the soldiers left. The officers' gardens end then too. Soldiers kept the field, and there were none at Chicago from that day to July 1816.

Was the house painted white, or is that just how the picture was drawn? We built it painted white, and that is our guess. The picture draws the walls smooth and pale, with no rows of logs and no corners. But it draws the boards of the shed in lines, the fence rails one by one, and the chimney's dark side. The artist drew rough parts where he saw them. So the pale wall is more likely paint than just a way of drawing. Lime wash on a log house was common on the frontier. No paper says this cabin was white. A gray picture drawn a hundred years later cannot prove it.

Two books say it in different words, but they put it on the same ground. Wau-Bun puts the house on the lake shore, not far from the fort. Currey puts it near the fort, on the bank of the river, across from where the river ran into the lake. He says that was near Madison Street and Michigan Avenue today. He gives the reason: a long sand bar kept the river from going straight out, so it ran south along the shore for a while. He also says Charles Lee's house stood on the river bank, near its mouth. Moses and Kirkland say it was south of the fort. On our 1812 ground, the river ran south behind the sand bar. At the place where it ran out, the river bank and the lake shore are the same bank. So the house stands there, and both writers are right. It is about 29 meters from where the river ran out and 22 meters from the lake shore, on the dry back of the beach. Madison Street is 80 meters south of the house. That fits the two ways people have read where the river's mouth was. Currey says the house was across from the river's mouth, and we kept that. If the mouth moves on our map, the house moves too. Which way the house faced is our guess.

Three books put this house at the foot of State Street, and one puts it closer to the lake. We go with the three. Wau-Bun says Burns's house stood near where the agent's house, Cobweb Castle, was built later, at the foot of North State Street. Moses and Kirkland say it was near the south-west corner of North State and Water Streets. Currey says Burns lived in a cabin on the north bank of the river near the State Street bridge, across from the creek. Hurlbut thought it was a log house two or three hundred yards from the lake and twenty steps from the river. On our ground, the lake is about 600 meters east of State Street. Two or three hundred yards from the lake would put it right where the Kinzie house is. Both cannot be true, and three writers give the street corner. From Hurlbut we keep one thing: twenty steps from the river. That fits the corner. So the south wall is about 15 meters north of the river bank. Moses and Kirkland name both corners, north-east and south-west. The south-west one is between Water Street and the river, so it keeps the twenty steps. The exact spot is our choice. It stands just west of the later agent's house, clear of it. Which way the house faced is our guess.

A picture from 1912 draws a zigzag rail fence along the river and round the field. It is a snake fence. The picture was made long after, so this is our best guess from it. It is also the kind of fence a frontier farm built when it had no tool to dig post holes.

This was the Burns family's house. The old books do not agree on the husband's first name, and we do not choose. Moses and Kirkland think he was probably the Thomas Burns on the fort's list of soldiers in 1810. That man joined on 8 June 1806, so he was due to leave the army on 8 June 1811. Currey calls him John Burns every time. Neither one says where the name comes from. Wau-Bun calls it only Burns's house.

This was the government's trading house. It sold goods to the Potawatomi and other nations for furs. The trade agent lived in it too. We worked out that this is that building. It is the house with a fence, right west of the fort. The Chicago Magazine of 1857 puts the two-story log trading house there. Quaife names two log houses a short way to the south-west. This is the one without the number 17.

The back of the dock is set at the height of the ground, so a man can walk off the bank onto the boards. The 1835 docks are built the same way. No paper says this. At the front of the dock, the water is less than a meter deep. That is enough for a small boat, or one bringing goods in from a ship out past the sand bar. It is not deep enough for the big ship.

The old map draws its front with two rows of windows. The Chicago Magazine of March 1857 says it too: the two-story log trading house west of the fort. That piece ends with: 'Such was the old Fort previous to 1812.' A web page quotes it. We can name that page, but we do not know if we may use it. So the two floors stand on the old map, and that is our best guess.
The old map draws one chimney, at the house's east end. Our house maker puts the chimney its own way, at no set end. So the east end is not kept.
The old map draws one chimney, at the house's west end. Our house maker puts the chimney its own way, at no set end. So the west end is not kept.

This was the farm's cabin. Lee's hired men lived here and worked the farm. Lee and his family lived in their own house near the fort, on the shore by the river's mouth. Currey tells of it. Heald calls it Russell and Lee's cabin, in a field.

The field's fence has the same dates as the cabin. It starts on 6 April 1812, when Heald's letter puts the cabin in a field by the river. It ends at the end of 1822 with the cabin. That end date is our choice. A field that grew food for the fort for a season or more was fenced to keep animals out. Wau-Bun says there were cows across the river. So we think the fence stood with the field.

These are the house's dates. It starts in the fall of 1804. Currey says John Kinzie bought the house from Le Mai that year and came that fall. Other books give other years, so we chose the later one. The house is older than that. Du Sable and Le Mai lived in it before, in a shape no picture shows. It stood in August 1812. Currey says the house was not burned when the others were. It ends at the end of 1833. Currey says it was torn down in the early 1830s. A picture from 1857 shows it about 1833. It was empty and falling down from 1832 and gone by 1835. So it is not in the 1835 town.

The old plan shows the main gate going from the inner fence out through this one. So this outer fence is open there too. We put the gate where the plan puts the way through, a little west of the middle of this side. Quaife says there was a small gate near the north-west tower. We could not find it on the plan at first. Now a picture by Currey, made long after, shows a west gate just south of the north-west tower. That fits Quaife. It does not tell us its exact place or width. The south gate did not change. The owner of this project said the soldiers in the covered walk should walk through the fence. So we added a small back gate, 1.5 meters wide, at this fence's north-east corner, lined up with the covered walk. Wau-Bun names a small back gate, and Quaife says the covered walk ran from the fort's north-east corner. The plan does not draw it. Its place, width and door are our guesses.

The front facing the river has nine openings. The 1912 picture draws them in this order from the down-river end: window, door, window, window, door, window, window, door, window. That makes three doors and six windows. We read each one closely off the picture and put it on the wall. Each is right to within about 20 centimeters. The picture was made long after, so this is our best guess, not a fact. Three doors is also what a house of two rooms under one roof would have.

The square of ground the flag pole stands on is half a meter on each side. That is the same as the second fort's pole, and the smallest we can build. The old map draws the pole lying flat, so it does not show how thick it was.

Not its color, just how dark it is. The 1912 picture draws the roof much darker than the walls, nearly black. That is how a roof of wood shingles, darkened by weather, looks in a gray picture. We made the roof weathered dark. No paper says what the roof was made of.

No paper gives its size. We sized it from the 1912 picture. The picture shows a long, low house. Its river side is about two and a half times as long as its end, with three doors and six windows. We made it 48 by 18 feet, or about 15 by 5.5 meters. The picture was made long after and gives no measures, so the size is our guess. A log house this long would be two rooms under one roof, and the three doors fit that. We build it as one.

No paper shows this. A roof with four sloped sides over a near-square building is the kind that survives. Whistler's plan says the lookouts were not yet built on the towers. The lookout that sits on top now has its own note, so it is not counted here.

No paper shows this. It is a garden gate in a fence of thin boards. It has two posts and one door made of the same boards, on two rails with a brace. It hangs on the west post and opens in. That is how a five-foot fence was gated. The fort's big heavy gates are for its tall wall. You can open this gate with Interact.

No paper shows this. There is a gate in front of the door, so the porch opens onto the green. The owner of this project wanted to walk into the front garden, so there is a second gate on the river side too, in line with it. That is where a path from the boat landing would come in. Both are our guesses.

No paper shows this. It is a gate in the fence of thin boards round the green. It has two posts and one door of the same boards, and it swings in, like the gate of the chief's garden. You can open it with Interact.

No paper shows this. This stack has dried and sagged since it was built. Its middle bulges out, and its top leans to one side. That is what a stack does when it was built a bit wet or on soft ground. Which stack stands which way is our choice. That way the four look like hay built and used by hand, not one shape four times.

No paper shows this. Hay has been pulled out of one side, right down to the ground. The brighter hay inside shows, and pulled hay lies in heaps at its foot. This is the old stack the farm fed from. In Wau-Bun, a soldier pulled some hay for the cows. Which stack stands which way is our choice. That way the four look like hay built and used by hand, not one shape four times.

No paper gives this. We read the roof's slope off the 1912 picture. At 30 degrees the roof was a bit too high for the picture. At 24 degrees it matches. That also leaves the chimney top just above the roof, as the picture shows it. The picture was made long after.

No paper shows this. This stack is round and full, drawn in to a point, and only a little settled. It was built this July and no one has touched it yet. Which stack stands which way is our choice. That way the four look like hay built and used by hand, not one shape four times.

No paper shows this. The cows loose among the stacks have eaten into its foot all round. So it stands on a thin waist under hanging hay. In Wau-Bun the stacks have no fence, and the cows stood among them. Which stack stands which way is our choice. That way the four look like hay built and used by hand, not one shape four times.

No paper gives this. In the 1912 picture the chimney top is a little above the roof. We made the chimney 4.2 meters tall. That puts its top about half a meter over the roof. That is the eighteen inches the 1835 town's rule asks of every chimney, and our check holds every building to it. The picture's own chimney is a little shorter. Our usual chimney would be taller, but this one is at the corner of the roof, not by its top.
No paper shows this. Two pairs of poles are tied over the top and lie down its sides. They hold the top down in the wind. That was a common way to weigh down a stack. We drew it on one of the four.

We are trying out a small west gate, 1.5 meters wide, cut through both fence rows. It sits in the gap just south of the north-west tower. We chose that spot from the buildings near it, not from the old map. Nothing else moves. The gate is a plain door of boards on rails, like our other small gates. Its width and the way it swings in are our guesses. This does not say when it was built. The owner of this project asked for a small back gate here too, 1.5 meters wide, in this fence's east side, between the chief's house and the small north-east house. It leads from the yard to the walk between the fence rows, and on to the covered walk. Its place, width and door are our guesses.

We are trying out a small west gate, 1.5 meters wide, cut through both fence rows. It sits in the gap just south of the north-west tower. We chose that spot from the buildings near it, not from the old map. Nothing else moves. The gate is a plain door of boards on rails, like our other small gates. Its width and the way it swings in are our guesses. This does not say when it was built. The owner of this project said the soldiers in the covered walk should walk through the fence. So we added a small back gate, 1.5 meters wide, at this fence's north-east corner, lined up with the covered walk. Wau-Bun names a small back gate, and Quaife says the covered walk ran from the fort's north-east corner. The plan does not draw it. Its place, width and door are our guesses.

The main gate in the south fence stands 2.6 meters (8.6 feet) west of the fence's middle. The old plan shows the way through the main gate in the gap between the two halves of the soldiers' houses. So the gate stands right in that gap. At first we could only put a gate in the middle. Then it hung across the back of the soldiers' house, with a wall behind it. Quaife says the gate was at the middle of the south side. That means in the middle of the row of houses, which the plan measures. The plan is good to about a foot.

The main gate in the south fence stands 2.8 meters (9.3 feet) west of the fence's middle. The old plan shows the way through the main gate in the gap between the two halves of the soldiers' houses. So the gate stands right in that gap. At first we could only put a gate in the middle. Then it hung across the back of the soldiers' house, with a wall behind it. Quaife says the gate was at the middle of the south side. That means in the middle of the row of houses, which the plan measures. The plan is good to about a foot.

Which house belonged to whom is our guess. Cooper, the fort's doctor from 1808, counted four houses on the north side. He says Kinzie, Ouilmette, La Lime and Le Mai lived in them. Whistler's map of January 1808 draws Kinzie's house and three more west of it, but names none. Quaife puts the two together. We gave Ouilmette the house nearest Kinzie's. Currey says his cabin was close behind the Kinzie house, and Wau-Bun says close at hand. The other two take Cooper's other names in his order, going west. La Lime gets the middle house and Le Mai the far west one. Cooper does not say his order is the order on the ground.

Old books say who lived in Ouilmette's house. Which house on the map was his is our guess. Currey says Ouilmette was a Frenchman. His wife was Native, a Potawatomi. He had lived here since 1790. She was given land on the north shore, where Wilmette is now. Currey also says her sister, Mrs. Bisson, lived with them. Wau-Bun says both women had Native and French parents. Victoire Porthier said some of her family lived in the Ouilmette house, across the river from the fort, before it burned. We say it is the house nearest Kinzie's. Currey puts his cabin close behind the Kinzie house. Wau-Bun says close at hand.

Wau-Bun tells of a big green yard with a fence, between the house and the river. When we compared our house and green with the old picture, the green was far too wide. It ran 13 meters past the west end of the house. Nothing showed it that wide. So we made it 17 meters wide: the house, with about 2.4 meters more at each end, around the same door. How far it runs back to the river did not change. The pictures show only its shape, not its size.

Wau-Bun says the garden ran north of the house. Whistler's map of 1808 draws the Kinzie house in a fenced yard marked as Mr. Kinzie's kitchen garden, with the old horse mill outside it to the west. So the garden lies north of the house and its yard of sheds, and east of the mill. Its corners are our guess.

Whistler's map of 25 January 1808 draws two small houses at the bottom left, where the river meets a branch. One is in the corner between the branch and the river, across from the fort. The other is on the fort's side, next to the corn field. Quaife says the map shows two houses at the fork, one lived in by a man who had left the army. The map's branch is the North Branch. This house is drawn across the main river from the fort, on the near side of the branch. So it stands on the north bank, east of the North Branch. We set it about 75 meters from the branch and 50 meters from the main river, so the water cannot reach it even if our river line is off. The map is not drawn to size here, so we claim nothing closer. Which way it faces is our guess.

Whistler's map of 25 January 1808 draws two small houses at the bottom left, where the river meets a branch. One is in the corner between the branch and the river, across from the fort. The other is on the fort's side, next to the corn field. Quaife says the map shows two houses at the fork, one lived in by a man who had left the army. This is the house on the fort's side of the river, next to the corn field's words. So it stands on the south bank of the main river, east of the South Branch. That is where Quaife puts the corn field. We set it about 45 meters from the main river and 70 meters from the South Branch, about 20 meters west of the corn field fence. The map is not drawn to size here, so we claim nothing closer. Which way it faces is our guess.

Whistler's plan marks number 7 as the Main Gate, in the middle of the south row of houses. Quaife says the main gate was at the middle of the south side. At first we could only put a gate in the middle. Now it stands where the plan puts the way through, about 8.6 feet west of the middle. Quaife says there was a small gate near the north-west tower. We could not find it on the plan at first. Now a picture by Currey, made long after, shows a west gate just south of the north-west tower. That fits Quaife. It does not tell us its exact place or width. The south gate did not change. The owner of this project asked for a small back gate here too, 1.5 meters wide, in this fence's east side, between the chief's house and the small north-east house. It leads from the yard to the walk between the fence rows, and on to the covered walk. Its place, width and door are our guesses.

It is laid in hand-made brick, like the fort's other brick. It is a soft red brick, baked in a pile, with wide lime between. Its color is a little darker than the brick on the map. That it is brick comes from the old papers. That it was soft hand-made brick of this color, laid this way, is our guess.

Our guess is 17 meters along the river and 15.5 meters back to the bank. The old 39 meter width did not match the old picture. The words about the house and its big green yard, and the family's own picture, guided this choice. We do not treat any drawing as an exact measure.

This is the part from the main roof up to the edge of the little roof on top. The owner of this project compared our first build with the fort's drawings. The lookouts looked about a fifth too tall. So we cut the body from 2.1 meters to 1.6 meters. That makes the whole lookout about a fifth shorter. Neither picture is drawn to size. This was judged by eye.
